lessons.title: Arrays and dtypes
lessons.intro: An ndarray is a block of memory holding one fixed type, plus a shape that says how to read it. Almost every numpy surprise is the dtype or the shape doing exactly what it was told.
takeaways: Every array has one dtype and one shape.
`/` gives floats, `//` keeps ints, small ints wrap around.
Vectorising removes interpreter overhead, not algorithmic work.
lessons.trap: Treating a `uint8` or `int32` array like Python's unbounded integers: overflow is silent and gives plausible wrong numbers.

sections.heading: One type per array
sections.text: Integers stay integers until something forces a float. `/` always yields floats; `//` keeps integers. The result dtype is the 'widest' of the operands.

sections.heading: Fixed width means wrap-around
sections.text: Small integer dtypes do not grow. A `uint8` image array that overflows wraps silently, so cast before arithmetic.

sections.heading: Why vectorise
sections.text: A loop in Python pays interpreter cost per element. A numpy call runs one compiled loop over packed numbers. The algorithm is the same, so the gain is a constant factor, usually large.
code: print(np.sum(x * x), sum(int(v) ** 2 for v in x))

lessons.title: Views and copies
lessons.intro: numpy avoids copying whenever it can describe the result as a different way of reading the same memory. That makes it fast, and it means editing one name can change another.
takeaways: Basic slices, transposes and reshapes are views.
List, integer-array and boolean indexing copy.
Copy before mutating a slice you do not own.
lessons.trap: Normalising `X[:, :3] /= s` in place when `X` is the caller's training data: you have just rewritten their dataset.

sections.heading: Basic slicing is a view
sections.text: Slices, `.T`, and `reshape` of contiguous data share the buffer. Writing through one name shows up in every other.

sections.heading: Fancy and boolean indexing copy
sections.text: Indexing with lists, integer arrays or masks gathers elements into a new array, so edits to the result do not touch the source.

sections.heading: Ask when unsure
sections.text: `np.shares_memory(a, b)` answers it directly. Call `.copy()` before mutating anything you did not just create.

lessons.title: Broadcasting and shapes
lessons.intro: Broadcasting is the rule that lets arrays of different shapes combine without loops. Learn the rule and shape errors become readable instead of mysterious.
takeaways: Align from the right; sizes must match or be 1.
`None` / `keepdims=True` add the size-1 axes that make broadcasting do what you mean.
Write the expected shape in a comment, and assert it.
lessons.trap: A silent broadcast: subtracting a `(n,)` vector from a `(n, 1)` column gives `(n, n)`, not an error and not what you wanted.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.text: Line the shapes up from the right. Each pair of sizes must be equal, or one of them must be 1 (that axis is stretched). Missing leading axes count as 1.

sections.heading: Pairwise tables for free
sections.text: Adding an axis with `None` turns a vector into a column, so a single expression builds every pairwise difference. This is the core of distance matrices and attention scores.

sections.heading: When it fails
sections.text: A mismatch with no 1 to stretch raises. Fix it by reshaping on purpose, not by guessing: `(3, 4) + (3,)` fails because the 3 aligns with the 4.

lessons.title: Axes, reductions and indexing
lessons.intro: `axis` names the dimension a reduction collapses. Once you can say that sentence for any call, indexing and reductions stop needing trial and error.
takeaways: `axis=k` removes axis k from the shape.
`keepdims=True` keeps it as size 1 so results broadcast back.
Masks select and assign; `argmax` takes the first tie.
lessons.trap: Taking the mean over the wrong axis still returns an array of plausible shape. Check the shape and a hand-computed row.

sections.heading: axis means 'collapse this one'
sections.text: Summing over axis 0 of a `(2, 3)` array collapses the rows and leaves three column totals; axis 1 leaves two row totals.

sections.heading: keepdims for normalising
sections.text: Keeping the collapsed axis as size 1 lets the result broadcast straight back. This is the row-normalisation idiom.

sections.heading: Masks and arg-functions
sections.text: A boolean mask selects (and, on the left of `=`, edits) elements. `argmax` returns the first maximum.

lessons.title: Numerical stability and random numbers
lessons.intro: Floats are finite approximations. Most ML bugs that print `nan` or drift slowly are one of three things: overflow, absorption or catastrophic cancellation.
takeaways: Subtract the max before `exp`; use `logsumexp` for logs of sums.
Compare floats with a tolerance and detect NaN with `isnan`.
Pass a seeded `Generator`; avoid global seeds.
lessons.trap: Assuming a seed fixes results across numpy versions: stream details can change between releases, so assert properties, not exact draws, in long-lived tests.

sections.heading: Overflow and the max trick
sections.text: `exp` overflows for inputs around 710 in float64 (far sooner in float16). Subtract the maximum and the largest exponent becomes 0.

sections.heading: Absorption and NaN
sections.text: Small numbers vanish next to large ones, and a NaN poisons everything it touches. Use `np.isnan`, never `==`.

sections.heading: Seeded generators
sections.text: Create one `Generator` per experiment and pass it down. The same seed gives the same stream, on any machine, for the same numpy version.
